title: Ramana's Forty Verses
hook: is the world real? two friends argue past midnight
tomorrow: every movie needs one thing nobody looks at. what is it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramana's Forty Verses opened: abiding as it is, is the meditation. Today a week of lamps and pictures comes back, plus one argument he won't join.

Two friends on the back steps, long past midnight. One has just watched a video: the world isn't real, it's all appearance. The other laughs: great, then pay my rent in appearance money. They go around for an hour. Ramana's verses have a line for exactly this argument, and it isn't a point for either side.
screen: `IS THE WORLD REAL?` → `AN HOUR ON THE BACK STEPS.` → `A POINT FOR NEITHER SIDE.`

segments.voice: Just before it, the second verse of Ulladu Narpadu says teachings begin with three: the world, the soul and God. The one reality shows up as three, Ramana says, only while the separate I lasts. Then the third verse, in paraphrase: the world is real; no, it's illusion. It's conscious; no, it isn't. It's happiness; no, it isn't. What use is all this arguing? Set the world aside, know the self, and rest where there's no one and no two. He doesn't win the debate. He moves it. Every claim about the world is made by someone, so before settling what the world is, find out who's looking. And that's the turn this whole week has made. A painted cloth under every figure. A tenth traveler who was doing the counting. A glow that leads to the real jewel. A lamp, the witness, still burning in an empty hall. The great sayings, weighed word by word. And Ramana's question about being. Different pictures, one turn: from the thing seen to the one seeing.
screen: `THREE, WHILE THE SEPARATE I LASTS.` · `WHAT USE IS ARGUING?` · `FIRST ASK WHO'S LOOKING.` · `A WEEK OF PICTURES, ONE TURN.` · then, large: `FROM THE SEEN TO THE ONE SEEING.`

segments.voice: Sit with your hands open on your knees or lap, palms up, as if setting something down. When a thought arrives carrying a verdict, this is real, this is pointless, let it rest in the open hands without arguing back. Then notice who the verdict was for.
Ramana's Forty Verses: a Tamil poem that keeps turning from the world to the one who sees it.
Keep this one: Ramana's Forty Verses, and before deciding what the world is, ask who's looking. A week of lamps, done.

screen: `DAY 1687 COUNTS.` → `RAMANA'S FORTY VERSES · 2 OF 7.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DOES NOBODY AT A MOVIE SEE?`

howItsDone: Ramana's followers read the verses slowly, often one at a time, and turn each one back on the reader with the question 'who am I?'
